The paper defines Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) as large‑scale, multimodal systems that generate low‑level actions and can be rapidly adapted across tasks, environments, and hardware via language, vision and proprioception.  Positioned at the top of a five‑level control taxonomy, RFMs aim to become generalist, zero‑/few‑shot, online‑adaptable agents for industrial use.  A systematic review assembled three corpora—1 263 publications, of which 1 025 are highly relevant RFM works (324 focus on manipulation) and 125 address industrial implications—revealing a rapid rise in RFM research but a notable lack of industrial‑focused surveys.

From this base the authors extracted eleven inter‑dependent industrial implications (I1‑I11) and refined them into 47 concrete attributes, forming a 149‑item criteria catalogue that spans model‑centric, ecosystem‑centric and hybrid requirements (e.g., multi‑hardware support, out‑of‑distribution robustness, calibrated uncertainty, human‑in‑the‑loop correction, safety gating, governance).  The catalogue was applied to the 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs via an automated GPT‑5.1‑based pipeline, producing 48 276 individual criterion decisions.  Expert‑LLM agreement was high (96.6 % accuracy, κ = 0.744) but showed a conservative bias (22.6 % false‑negative rate).

Quantitatively, total industrial‑applicability scores for all RFMs were ≤ 0.12, with most ≤ 0.05, indicating that on average a model satisfies roughly one‑tenth of the catalogue’s criteria.  The five highest‑scoring systems reached only 0.11–0.12; the best single‑implication score was 0.44 for adaptability (I1) achieved by Gemini Robotics 1.5.  Top models typically excel in two or three implications—most often adaptability (I1), robustness (I4), sensor fusion (I9) or data efficiency (I11)—while scoring near zero on safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time operation (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7).

Breadth–depth analysis showed that research from 2020‑2025 concentrates on adaptability (I1), benchmarking (I10) and data usage (I11), with ≈ 75 % of papers mentioning these but covering less than 10 % of the detailed items within each.  Even the top‑50 most‑cited papers improve breadth only modestly (≈ 23 % depth for the three dominant implications).  Safety, HRI, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness remain persistently under‑addressed (ACC < 0.05), revealing a gap between acknowledged industrial constraints and concrete solutions.

Hardware context is provided: typical cobots have 6‑axis arms, 8.5 kg payload, ≈0.1 mm accuracy and ≈0.3 kW power, while edge compute options range from low‑power NVIDIA Jetson Orin‑Nano (≈148 TOPS $/) to high‑end RTX 5090 (>120 W).  These constraints demand low‑latency, energy‑efficient inference, which current RFMs do not yet satisfy holistically.

The authors conclude that RFMs hold promise for multi‑task competence and cross‑domain generalisation, yet existing models deliver isolated capabilities without integrated safety monitoring, deterministic real‑time execution, or cost‑effective hardware integration.  They recommend layered architectures separating planning, verification and safety, edge‑aware benchmarking that includes latency, logging and dynamic sensor/tool changes, and focused research on the under‑served implications (I2, I3, I6, I7).  Limitations include reliance on an automated LLM extraction pipeline, absence of confidence intervals, and unreconstructed tables, restricting fine‑grained numeric reporting.  Overall, the audit shows modest progress on adaptability and data efficiency but a substantial gap before RFMs can be considered industry‑grade, autonomous solutions.
